facts.statement: Fossils of Tonsala are found in Late Oligocene terrains in the State of Washington and Japan.
facts.quote: The genus is known from terrains dated from the Late Oligocene of the State of Washington and Japan.

facts.statement: The type species Tonsala hildegardae was formally described in 1980 by Storrs L. Olson based on fossils collected by Douglas Emlong from the Pysht Formation on the Olympic Peninsula.
facts.quote: The Washington fossils, collected by Douglas Emlong in Late Oligocene terrains of the Pysht Formation, in the north of the Olympic Peninsula, were formally described the next year, 1980, by Olson himself, as the type of the new genus and species Tonsala hildegardae.

facts.statement: In 1979, Storrs L. Olson and Hasegawa Yoshikazu identified fossils from Washington and Japan as a distinct genus within the family Plotopteridae.
facts.quote: In 1979, Storrs L. Olson and Hasegawa Yoshikazu identified several fossilized specimens of Late Oligocene and Early Miocene birds found in the State of Washington and in Japan as members of the family Plotopteridae, but distinct enough from Plotopterum in their general anatomy to warrant their own genus.

facts.statement: A new species, Tonsala buchanani, was proposed in 2011 based on Oligocene fossils from the Pysht and Makah Formations.
facts.quote: In 2011, Gareth J. Dyke, Xia Wang and Michael B. Habib proposed a new species based on Oligocene fossils found in the Pysht Formation and the underlying Makah Formation, Tonsala buchanani.

facts.statement: Remains from Japan that were tentatively assigned to a new Tonsala species in 1996 were redescribed in 2019 as a new genus and species, Stenornis kanmonensis.
facts.quote: In 2019, the Japanese remains assigned tentatively to a new species of Tonsala by Olson and Hasegawa in 1996 were redescribed and assigned to a new genus and species, Stenornis kanmonensis

facts.statement: In 2021, the species Tonsala buchanani was transferred to the genus Klallamornis, where it became the type species.
facts.quote: In 2021, T. buchanani was moved to the genus Klallamornis by Mayr and Goedert, as K. buchanani, becoming the new type species of the genus.

facts.statement: In 2016, Mayr and Goedert referred specimens from the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene of the Jansen Creek Member of the Makah Formation to Tonsala, including a partial pelvis tentatively assigned to T. hildegardae and a coracoid tentatively referred as ?Tonsala sp.
facts.quote: In 2016, Mayr and Goedert referred two additional specimens from the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene of the Jansen Creek Member of the Makah Formation to the genus Tonsala, including one partial pelvis collected in 2004 by Goedert, tentatively assigned to T. hildegardae, and a right coracoid collected in 2009 by D. W. Starr tentatively referred to the genus as ?Tonsala sp.

facts.statement: In 2017, Mayr and Goedert established the clade Tonsalinae with Tonsala as the type genus, including derived plotopterids except for Phocavis, Stemec, and Plotopterum.
facts.quote: In 2017, Mayr and Goedert used Tonsala as the type genus of the new clade Tonsalinae, comprising all derived Plotopterids, aside from the primitive and fragmentary Phocavis and the small-sized Stemec and Plotopterum

facts.statement: In 2017, a partial skeleton of T. hildegardae containing the first known tarsometatarsus for the genus was referred to Tonsala by Mayr and Goedert.
facts.quote: In 2017, Mayr and Goedert used Tonsala as the type genus of the new clade Tonsalinae, comprising all derived Plotopterids, aside from the primitive and fragmentary Phocavis and the small-sized Stemec and Plotopterum; they additionally referred to the genus, as a new specimen of T. hildegardae, a partial skeleton including most notably the first known tarsometatarsus assigned to the genus.

facts.statement: Tonsala hildegardae was a large, flightless seabird comparable in size to a great penguin and larger than its relative Plotopterum.
facts.quote: Tonsala hildegardae was a large and flightless seabird, comparable in size with a great penguin, and larger than its later relative Plotopterum.

facts.statement: Tonsala was heavily adapted for swimming and diving, featuring paddle-shaped wings and a scapula with a thin, expanded blade similar to penguins to aid propulsion.
facts.quote: The genus was heavily adapted towards swimming and diving; the wings were paddle-shaped, and the scapula had a thin and expanded blade, similar to that of penguins, to help the animal propel through water.

facts.statement: The wing structure of Tonsala, particularly the humerus and radius, shows convergent evolution resembling early penguins and flightless auks rather than its related Pelecaniformes.
facts.quote: The structure of the wing, and notably the shape of the humerus and radius, shared more resemblances with early penguins and flightless auks like Pinguinus and Mancalla than with the related Pelecaniformes, in a case of convergent evolution.

facts.statement: The ulna of Tonsala shares similarities with the unrelated Paleocene penguin Waimanu.
facts.quote: The ulna itself shared similarities with the unrelated Paleocene penguin Waimanu.

facts.statement: The pelvis of Tonsala was broad, shallow, and elongated with a praeacetabular portion twice the size of the postacetabular portion, resembling the pelvis of modern darters.
facts.quote: The pelvis of Tonsala was broad and shallow, more elongated than that of Copepteryx, and reduced in its caudal portion; it shared similarities with the pelvis of modern darters, and was characterized by an elongated praeacetabular portion, twice as large than the postacetabular portion.

facts.statement: The caudal vertebrae of Tonsala were large, twice the size of those found in the modern great cormorant.
facts.quote: The caudal vertebrae were large, twice the size of those of the modern great cormorant.

facts.statement: The complete beak of Tonsala was presumably proportionally longer than modern relatives and featured elongated, very narrow nostrils, unlike modern Suloids which have greatly reduced or absent nostrils.
facts.quote: The complete beak was presumably proportionally longer than those of its modern relatives, and was opened by elongated and very narrow nostrils, unlike modern Suloids for which the nostrils are greatly reduced or completely absents.

facts.statement: The skull of Tonsala was devoid of a vomer bone.
facts.quote: The skull was devoid of vomer.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that Phocavis maritimus may be synonymous with Tonsala hildegardae.
facts.quote: it has been suggested that Phocavis maritimus may be synonymous with Tonsala hildegardae.

facts.statement: Following criticism of Dyke et al. (2016), Mayr and Goedert tentatively referred one partial skeleton previously assigned to the type species as cf. Tonsala hildegardae.
facts.quote: Additional criticism of Dyke et al, 2016 led to a reevaluation of the specimens assigned to Tonsala; one of the partial skeletons referred to the type species by Dyke et al. was only tentatively referred by Mayr and Goedert, as cf. Tonsala hildegardae.

facts.statement: The species name hildegardae was given to honor Hildegarde Howard, the American paleontologist who described Plotopterum.
facts.quote: the species name, hildegardae, was given to honour Hildegarde Howard, the American paleontologist who described Plotopterum.

facts.statement: Tonsala was first described by Olson in 1980 as a member of the clade Sulae.
facts.quote: In 1980, Olson, describing the first remains of Tonsala as member of the clade Sulae

facts.statement: In 2017, Mayr and Goedert proposed the clade Tonsalinae to include Tonsala and other large plotopterids.
facts.quote: In 2017, Mayr and Goedert proposed a new clade, Tonsalinae, including Tonsala and all larger plotopterids known at the time

facts.statement: Within the clade Tonsalinae, Tonsala is considered the most basal member.
facts.quote: Within Tonsalinae, Tonsala was perceived as the most basal member

facts.statement: Tonsala lived between 33.9 and 23.04 million years ago, during the Rupelian to Chattian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Chattian (33.9 to 23.04 million years ago)

facts.statement: Tonsala was one of the smallest and most common plotopterids living along the Pacific Northwest coast during the Oligocene.
facts.quote: Although it was much larger than modern cormorants and darters, Tonsala was one of the smallest and the most common plotopterid living alongside the coast of the Pacific Northwest during the Oligocene

facts.statement: Tonsala likely propelled itself in water using wing upstroke movements with a force comparable to modern penguins.
facts.quote: The compressed wing elements and the extended scapular blade of Tonsala indicates that it was likely capable of producing wing upstroke movements to propulsate itself in water, with a force comparable to that of modern penguins

facts.statement: The enlarged patella in Tonsala suggests it stood upright on land like modern penguins and cormorants.
facts.quote: The enlarged patella present in the hindlimbs of Tonsala indicates that plotopterid assumed an upright posture on land, like modern penguins and cormorants

facts.statement: Cow shark teeth found with Tonsala fossils suggest that sharks fed on the carcasses of these birds.
facts.quote: Cow sharks teeth have also been recovered in association with Tonsala remains, suggesting they also fed on the carcasses of plotopterids

facts.statement: There are four recorded fossil occurrences of Tonsala in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 4

facts.statement: The exact phylogenetic relationships of plotopterids, including Tonsala, with modern bird taxa remain debated.
facts.quote: the exact status of their relationships with modern taxa is however still debated

facts.statement: In 2004, Gerald Mayr hypothesized that plotopterids were the sister group to modern penguins, a theory that has since been heavily criticized.
facts.quote: In 2004, Gerald Mayr tried to introduce an hypothesis on presumed phylogenetic relationships between the plotopterids and the modern penguins
